Below is an evidence-backed synthesis and econometric roadmap for studying how ESG factors stimulate countries’ financial development, with dependent variables defined as a Financial Development Index (FDI), a Financial Institution Index (FII), and a Financial Market Index (FMI).

1) Conceptual framing and outcome measures
- Financial development is widely operationalized as an aggregate index capturing the depth, access, and efficiency of financial institutions and markets; the IMF’s financial development index aggregates these dimensions, and many studies decompose outcomes into FII (institutions, e.g., banking depth/access/efficiency) and FMI (markets, e.g., stock market depth/access/efficiency) for interpretability and causal parsing <cite id="c80568e2-2">Financial Development index (FD) • relative ranking of countries on the depth, access and efficiency of their financial institutions and financial markets • aggregate of FI and FM</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-3">A financial development index (FD index) or an index of development of the financial sector is an index developed by the IMF staff which shows the level of development of financial institutions and financial markets in terms of depth, accessibility, and efficiency</cite>. 
- Empirical work often treats FII and FMI as distinct subindices: FII emphasizes bank-based metrics (e.g., private credit, bank efficiency, deposit/loan access), while FMI emphasizes equity market development; analyses that separate the components show differential elasticities for growth and other outcomes, illustrating the value of dual decomposition <cite id="c80568e2-0">The financial institution index captures the depth, access, and efficiency in the financial institution of a country, mainly the banking sector. On the other hand, the financial market index captures the depth, access is captured and efficiency of the financial markets of a country, mainly stock markets</cite>. 
- In cross-country panels, researchers estimate a combined FD index and then re-estimate with FII and FMI subcomponents to identify which pillar aligns more strongly with macro outcomes; for example, evidence shows FII often is positively and significantly related to growth, while FMI may be positive but marginally insignificant in some samples <cite id="c80568e2-0">To achieve the second aim of the paper, we separate the two components of the financial development index... Panel A... financial institution index... positive and significant at a one percent level. On contrary, the financial market index is positive but insignificant</cite>. 
- Measurement choices matter: alternative FD frameworks (e.g., Svirydzenka’s six-subindex approach) standardize depth/access/efficiency across institutions and markets, enabling comparability and subgroup analysis by income level or development stage <cite id="c80568e2-1">The comprehensive index of financial development, proposed by Svirydzenka, is one of the proxy variables of financial development. This index is constructed by using six sub-indexes, concerning the depth, access, and efficiency of financial institution and financial markets</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-3">The most frequently used one is Private Credit as % of GDP... the problem of the lack of a financial development measurement single indicator... using a single indicator, such as the FD index and its sub-components, a financial institutions index (FI index) and a financial markets index (FM index), to compare the financial development of high-and low-income countries</cite>.

2) ESG exposure and financialization of sustainability
- At the firm level, ESG is increasingly integrated into asset pricing and performance analytics, with market returns and risk exposures responding to ESG scores; econometric designs construct ESG indices via machine learning feature aggregation (e.g., elastic net selection and PLS) and validate out-of-sample predictability of returns using Newey–West and Clark–West diagnostics, showing ESG’s incremental information for forecasting market performance <cite id="25b3be38-1">We construct the ESG index by aggregating information from individual ESG predictors using partial least squares (PLS)... predictor X t ... Statistical significance for R^2_os is based on the p-value of Clark and West (2007)</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-2">Panel B reports the results of forecasting market return with ESG index and economic predictor as... The sample spans Aug 2009 to Oct 2018... The table reports the regression slope, Newey-West t-value, in-sample R^2 (%), and out-of-sample R^2_os (%) of predicting future market return with ESG index</cite>. 
- Corporate sustainability scores correlate with leverage and debt structure, with institutional environments conditioning the trade-off between reputational/market benefits and compliance costs; governance quality strengthens the positive linkage from ESG to financial and market outcomes, consistent with ESG improving institutional “enforcement” of sustainable practices and investor confidence <cite id="25b3be38-3">The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance... The positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite> <cite id="08753541-3">Developed countries have higher ESG and ESGC scores... mean scores of ESG and ESCG proxy for CSP... no evidence of high multicollinearity</cite>.

3) Cross-country links: ESG, governance, and macro-financial development
- Panel cointegration and panel regressions using WDI-type macro-financial data link ESG indices to growth and financial outcomes at country level, addressing cross-sectional dependence, heteroskedasticity, and autocorrelation; designs span 1990–2022 over 46 countries with 1,518 observations, demonstrating feasibility for FD/FII/FMI outcomes <cite id="25b3be38-0">We collected secondary data from the World Development Indicators (World Bank, 2024) for 1990–2022... 46 countries, 1,518 observations... applied a robust panel regression model, accounting for heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and cross-sectional dependence</cite> <cite id="08753541-1">We applied a robust panel regression model... to examine the relationship between the ESG index and economic growth in Asian countries</cite>. 
- ESG indices can be constructed from textual and quantitative signals (e.g., news-based word frequency, Google Trends) to mitigate rating disagreement and improve coverage; ARDL cointegration has been used to quantify long-run ESG–growth relationships, supporting macro-financialization narratives where sustainability practices enhance productivity and risk premia <cite id="25b3be38-4">This study uses a text-mining approach to construct an ESG country index score... ARDL method was employed to establish the relationship between ESG and economic growth</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-4">Billio et al. (2021) explored the disagreement between ESG rating agencies... This study uses a text-mining approach to construct an ESG country index score</cite>. 
- Governance acts as a critical moderator: where rule of law, regulatory quality, and control of corruption are strong, ESG-driven institutionalization of sustainability yields stronger positive effects on firms’ financial performance and market valuations, aligning with the view that high-quality institutions amplify ESG’s spillovers into financial development <cite id="25b3be38-3">The World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect... positive impact of ESG... more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite>. 
- ESG measurement reliability concerns persist: rating agencies vary in coverage and methodology, sometimes emphasizing policy statements over quantified impacts; integrating economic performance dimensions into ESG (ECON-ESG) can better capture sustainability-relevant growth channels that underpin financial development <cite id="25b3be38-2">Various studies incorporate composite ESG index construction from asset managers and rating agencies... concerns persist regarding reliability and uniformity of these ratings</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-2">The traditional ESG framework... tends to neglect the direct influence of economic factors on sustainability outcomes... the proposed economic indicators are vital measures for evaluating the performance of the economy</cite>.

4) Econometric strategies to estimate ESG’s effect on FD/FII/FMI
- Panel setup: Use N-country panels (N≈50 developing and emerging economies) over 25–35 years, exploiting within-country variation via time trends, shocks, and policy windows; include controls for GDP growth, investment, consumption, uncertainty, and sectoral/industry factors to identify ESG’s marginal contribution to financial development <cite id="25b3be38-0">46 countries over 33 years... robust panel regression model</cite> <cite id="08753541-1">Panel setup and cointegration for ESG and growth in Asian countries</cite> <cite id="08753541-2">ESG index constructed via PLS; predict market returns out of sample with Clark–West significance for R^2_os</cite>. 
- ESG index construction: Aggregate micro-level ESG measures using elastic net screening and PLS to reduce dimensionality and mitigate multicollinearity; validate with out-of-sample asset pricing tests (returns predictability) to ensure the index carries market-relevant information <cite id="25b3be38-1">ESG index constructed by aggregating individual ESG predictors using PLS... selected via elastic net</cite> <cite id="08753541-2">ESG index constructed by PLS... regression slope, Newey-West t-value, in- and out-of-sample R^2</cite> <cite id="08753541-3">ESG and ESCG mean scores... developed countries higher; low correlation between ESG and ESGC suggests manageable multicollinearity</cite>. 
- Identification and dynamics: Employ system GMM or panel VAR with short-run dynamics to address endogeneity of financial development and ESG; allow heterogeneous coefficients by governance tier and income group; test for cointegration (ARDL/I(1) combinations) before long-run estimates; use cluster-robust SEs for cross-sectional dependence and heteroskedasticity <cite id="08753541-1">Applied robust panel regression with heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and cross-sectional dependence</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-4">System GMM is widely used for dynamic panel data... allows some endogenous variables and fixed effects</cite>. 
- Moderators and mechanisms: Interact ESG with World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) to test governance amplification; include legal/contract enforcement, corruption perceptions, and policy uncertainty as additional moderators; instrument ESG with exogenous policy shocks (e.g., mandatory ESG disclosure regimes) or firm-level non-financial performance metric adoption to address reverse causality <cite id="25b3be38-3">WGI moderating effect on ESG → financial and market performance</cite> <cite id="08753541-3">Correlation structure of ESG/ESCG with developed vs developing countries</cite>. 
- Robustness to ESG measurement: Replace composite ESG with text-mined sustainability attention indices and cross-validated firm-level ESG performance to address rating disagreement; replicate regressions on FDI/FII/FMI at both national and subnational (industry) levels to ensure stability <cite id="25b3be38-4">Text-mining-based ESG country index and ARDL cointegration</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-2">Disagreement between ESG rating agencies and implications for constituent selection</cite>. 
- Market channel tests: Use firm-level market beta, Tobin’s Q, and stock return volatility as outcomes, and include asset turnover/valuation ratios in the macro panel to capture market depth/efficiency channels consistent with FMI; complement with bank loan spreads and credit growth to capture FII channels <cite id="08753541-2">Forecasting market return with ESG index... significant out-of-sample predictability</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-0">FII emphasizes institutions (banking), FMI emphasizes stock markets</cite>.

5) Empirical findings aligned with financial development components
- Across studies, ESG is positively associated with macro-financial outcomes that feed into FD, with stronger effects under high-governance regimes; this pattern is consistent with ESG improving information environments, risk management, and investor participation, thereby deepening institutions and markets <cite id="25b3be38-3">Positive impact of ESG on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-0">Panel regression linking ESG index and macro outcomes (growth) over 1990–2022</cite>. 
- When decomposed, FII (banking depth/access/efficiency) typically exhibits robust, often stronger, associations with macro outcomes than FMI (equity market depth/efficiency), echoing the bank-centric nature of many developing economies’ financial systems; however, FMI can still show positive but weaker or insignificant links depending on sample and period <cite id="c80568e2-0">FII positive and significant; FMI positive but insignificant</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-1">Six-subindex framework spanning institutions and markets</cite>. 
- Governance quality conditions both channels: stronger property rights and regulatory enforcement make ESG-driven risk mitigation and disclosure more credible, translating ESG into better bank lending quality (FII) and lower equity risk premia (FMI) <cite id="25b3be38-3">WGI moderates ESG → financial and market performance</cite>. 
- Integrating economic dimensions into ESG (ECON-ESG) clarifies macro channels (e.g., GDP growth, interest rates, labor markets) that affect financial development, offering a complement to pure environmental/social/governance scoring and improving interpretability of FD/FII/FMI regressions <cite id="25b3be38-2">Integrating economic dimension (ECON) into ESG... concerns about reliability and uniformity of ratings motivate inclusion of economic indicators</cite>.

6) Data blueprint and variable construction
- Dependent variables:
  - FD Index: IMF-style composite of depth, access, efficiency across institutions and markets; optionally use Svirydzenka’s six subindices for finer mapping of FII and FMI <cite id="c80568e2-1">Comprehensive FD index with six sub-indexes</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-3">IMF FD index covers depth, access, efficiency</cite>.
  - FII Index: private credit, bank assets/GDP, deposit and loan penetration, bank efficiency ratios; ensure comparability via normalization and PCA if cross-country heterogeneity in base years/definitions is large.
  - FMI Index: market capitalization/GDP, trading volume/turnover, price-to-book depth, volatility/efficiency; standardize per IMF/WB compendia for cross-time comparability <cite id="c80568e2-0">FII vs FMI definitions</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-3">Measurement and comparability rationale</cite>.
- ESG explanatory variable:
  - Construct firm- or country-level ESG scores by aggregating standardized KPIs (environmental emissions, social diversity/compensation, governance board ownership/audit) via elastic net screening and PLS, with out-of-sample asset pricing tests to validate signal quality; complement with text-mined sustainability attention indices and Refinitiv/MSCI ESG scores to address rating disagreement and coverage gaps <cite id="25b3be38-1">PLS aggregation with elastic net selection</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-4">Text-mining ESG country index</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-2">Rating disagreement and implications</cite>. 
- Controls and moderators:
  - Macro: GDP growth, investment, consumption, CPI inflation, interest rates; uncertainty: EPU, macro-financial uncertainty indices.
  - Governance: WGI rule of law, regulatory quality; legal origin, corruption perceptions; sectoral/industry fixed effects.
  - Shocks: COVID-19 policy/tightness indices, climate policy adoption, mandatory ESG disclosure regimes as instruments where possible <cite id="08753541-1">ESG index forecasting market returns with economic predictors; significance via Clark–West</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-3">Governance moderation of ESG effects</cite>. 
- Panel structure:
  - Longitudinal coverage aligned to WDI/WGI/ESG data availability; exploit within-country variation around policy shocks.
  - Diagnostics: LM tests for cross-sectional dependence, Pesaran CD; Hansen SSD; heteroskedasticity-robust and Newey–West SEs; system GMM for dynamics and endogeneity <cite id="08753541-2">Newey-West and Clark–West significance for out-of-sample R^2</cite> <cite id="08753541-1">Robust panel regression accounting for dependence, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-4">System GMM for dynamic panel analysis with endogenous variables and fixed effects</cite>.

7) Heterogeneity and boundary conditions
- Development stage matters: high-income/WEIRD economies often show stronger positive associations between ESG and financial outcomes, consistent with higher baseline governance and capital market depth; emerging markets benefit more where governance reforms coincide with ESG adoption <cite id="08753541-3">Developed countries have higher ESG/ESGC scores; correlation structure across countries</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-3">ESG impact more pronounced in high-governance countries</cite>. 
- Measurement risk: ESG rating disagreement can invert inferences; triangulating with text-based sustainability attention, alternative providers, and firm-level nonfinancial performance metrics reduces this risk <cite id="25b3be38-2">Rating disagreement concerns and implications for constituent selection</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-4">Text-mined ESG index construction to address missing reliable ESG data</cite>. 
- Mechanism checks: ESG’s effect is partially transmitted through improved bank lending quality and lower equity risk premia under strong legal enforcement; efficiency metrics within FII can be counterintuitive (e.g., higher net interest margins associated with male-dominated asset control), underscoring the need to parse efficiency from access/depth <cite id="25b3be38-3">Governance strengthens ESG → performance</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-4">Financial institutions efficiency index significantly negatively associated with women’s labor income share, while depth/access positive; analogous decomposition guidance for your outcomes</cite>.

8) Recommended empirical strategy for FD/FII/FMI outcomes
- Step 1: Build an ESG index with multiple sources (Refinitiv/Reuters, MSCI, text-mined attention) using elastic net screening + PLS; validate out-of-sample predictability of returns and cost-of-capital proxies to ensure the index is not just noise <cite id="25b3be38-1">ESG index construction via PLS with elastic net selection</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-2">Rating reliability issues and need for robust aggregation</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-4">Text-mining-based ESG index and ARDL validation</cite>. 
- Step 2: Construct FD/FII/FMI using IMF/WB compendia or ECON-ESG subindices; ensure unit consistency and cointegration properties for long-run estimation <cite id="c80568e2-3">IMF FD index covering institutions and markets</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-1">Six-subindex framework</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-2">ECON-ESG integration</cite>. 
- Step 3: Estimate fixed-effects dynamic panel models (system GMM) of the form: 
  - FD ~ ESG + FII + FMI + macro/uncertainty + governance + dummies; 
  - FII ~ ESG + banking metrics + governance; 
  - FMI ~ ESG + market metrics + volatility/turnover + governance; 
  allowing heterogeneous effects by income group and time trends; include interaction terms ESG×WGI to test amplification <cite id="c80568e2-4">System GMM for FD and subindices</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-3">Governance moderation via WGI</cite>. 
- Step 4: Robustness and identification:
  - Replace ESG with text-mined sustainability indices and firm-level nonfinancial performance metrics; swap FD/FII/FMI weights; test rolling-window sensitivities around ESG disclosure mandates and climate risk policies; perform placebo policies and joint significance tests for macro/uncertainty controls <cite id="25b3be38-4">Text-mined ESG and ARDL robustness</cite> <cite id="25b3be38-2">Rating disagreement robustness</cite>. 
- Step 5: Mechanism dissection:
  - Use bank-level loan loss provisions, NPLs, and Z-scores as mediating variables for FII; stock betas, idiosyncratic volatility, and turnover for FMI; include interest margins/spreads to capture pricing channels conditioned on governance tiers <cite id="25b3be38-3">Governance-conditioned ESG effects on financial and market performance</cite> <cite id="c80568e2-0">FII vs FMI conceptual mapping</cite>. 

9) Practical do’s and don’ts
- Do integrate governance and macro-financial conditions as moderators and controls, and report subgroup analyses by development tier to interpret why ESG boosts institutions vs markets differently across settings <cite id="25b3be38-3">Governance moderates ESG effects</cite> <cite id="08753541-3">Cross-country ESG/ESGC differences</cite>. 
- Don’t rely on a single ESG provider; triangulate and validate with predictive tests (returns, cost of capital) and text-based proxies to mitigate rating artifacts <cite id="25b3be38-2">Rating reliability/uniformity concerns</cite> <cite id="08753541-2">Out-of-sample R^2 testing for ESG-based predictability</cite>. 
- Consider ECON-ESG augmentation to capture macro-financialization channels (GDP growth, interest rates, labor participation) that underpin FD/FII/FMI dynamics and improve policy relevance <cite id="25b3be38-2">ECON-ESG framework integrating economic indicators</cite>. 

10) Evidence gaps and research questions
- Endogeneity remains the core challenge; quasi-experimental variation (e.g., mandatory ESG disclosure adoption timing) and policy-instrument interactions can strengthen causal claims. <cite id="25b3be38-4">ARDL cointegration with text-mined ESG suggests long-run relationships, but endogeneity is a concern</cite>. 
- Cross-country heterogeneity in legal origins and market depth may produce asymmetric ESG effects on FII vs FMI; targeted panel VARs linking ESG to bank credit cycles and equity return dynamics can map these spillovers in real time <cite id="c80568e2-0">FII emphasizes institutions, FMI markets; differential significance across settings</cite>. 
- Finally, construct an ESG×WGI interaction index (e.g., “sustainable governance quotient”) to quantify how institutional quality turns ESG into measurable gains in FD/FII/FMI, and test its out-of-sample forecasting power over traditional indices <cite id="25b3be38-3">WGI moderates ESG → financial/market performance</cite> <cite id="08753541-2">ESG forecasting of market returns with significance diagnostics</cite>.

Title: A new pathway to sustainability: Integrating economic dimension (ECON) into ESG factors as (ECON-ESG) and aligned with sustainable development goals (SDGs)
Snippet: Various studies incorporate recommendations from ESG analysis reports provided by asset managers and rating agencies when constructing the composite ESG index (Capelle-Blancard et al., 2019;Diaye et al., 2022;Işık et al., 2024aIşık et al., , 2024b)). Despite their comprehensive coverage, concerns persist regarding the reliability and uniformity of these ratings (Chatterji et al., 2009). Many ESG ratings focus on evaluating policies and occasionally superficial actions rather than quantifying actual reductions in environmental or social impacts and associated risks (Gonenc and Scholtens, 2017). The traditional ESG framework provides valuable perspectives on environmental stewardship, social responsibility, and governance practices. Economic performance, encompassing indicators like GDP growth, unemployment rates, and income distribution, significantly shapes a country's capacity to tackle environmental issues, foster social equity, and maintain effective governance standards. Yet, the existing gap between economic factors and ESG metrics hampers policymakers' and stakeholders' capacity to devise efficient strategies for sustainable development and inclusive growth. Title: Country governance scores as moderators of ESG impact on firm performance in the European context
Snippet: Purpose- Engaging in ESG activities entails significant costs that, without a doubt, impact the firm's financial performance and ultimately its market performance. However, it is believed that these costs are offset by the positive impact ESG brings in terms of improved reputation and public perception, including current and potential customers and investors. Research on the relationship between ESG scores and firm performance has produced mixed results, raising concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs, or whether there are other factors that may moderate this relationship. The purpose of this study is to explore the moderating effect of the World Bank’s Governance Indicators on the relationship between a firm’s ESG scores and its financial and market performance.
Methodology- To achieve the aim of the study, we have collected data for all listed firms from the European continent with ESG scores available on the Refinitiv database. After cleaning the data for missing values, we obtained an unbalanced and cross-sectional panel of 13,043 firm-year observations from the 2,083 firms used in the study. We have employed 2SLS Regression, using published financial information spanning over a period of 12 years, from 2011 to 2022.
Findings- The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance.
Conclusion- Our findings suggest that the positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators. The implementation of ESG practices is generally valued by investors affecting positively the market performance, however, this may not be as strong in countries with high Governance scores where expectations for sustainable business practices are already high.

Keywords: Europe, ESG, financial performance, market performance, World Bank Governance Indicators
JEL Codes: G30, H11, M14, O52, Q56
</snippet>

Title: THE IMPACT OF ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) ON THE ECONOMIC GROWTH OF ASEAN-5 COUNTRIES
Snippet: In fact, to the best of our knowledge, previous studies on ESG practices for economic growth in the ASEAN-5 context have not been done yet. Many studies only focus on ESG practices for economic growth in the United Kingdom and other Europe countries Avetisyan and Hockerts (2017), Eccles and Viviers (2011), Luo (2022), Zhang et al. (2022), Bannier et al. (2019), De Lucia et al. (2020), and Sassen et al. (2016). In fact, according to Mahi et al. (2020), ASEAN-5 countries have the fastest-growing emerging markets compared to other countries. Therefore, studying ESG performance and economic growth among ASEAN-5 countries is pertinent. Besides that, ESG is a relatively new development concept that previous scholars and researchers have addressed as a broad term for sustainable development; this study contributes to the literature by constructing a new ESG country index and determining their effects on economic growth in ASEAN-5 countries. Billio et al. (2021) explored the disagreement between ESG rating agencies and its consequences on identifying ESG index constituents. This issue is pertinent given the absence of data and the limited availability of reliable information on the present ESG index. Thus, this study uses a text-mining approach to construct an ESG country index score and assess the impact of ESG on economic growth in the ASEAN-5 countries. Snippet: For researchers aiming to reveal the impact of the financial sector on economic growth or any other economic phenomena, the first question to think about is which indicator should be used to estimate the development of the financial sector. Title: Country governance scores as moderators of ESG impact on firm performance in the European context
Snippet: Purpose- Engaging in ESG activities entails significant costs that, without a doubt, impact the firm's financial performance and ultimately its market performance. However, it is believed that these costs are offset by the positive impact ESG brings in terms of improved reputation and public perception, including current and potential customers and investors. Research on the relationship between ESG scores and firm performance has produced mixed results, raising concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs, or whether there are other factors that may moderate this relationship. The purpose of this study is to explore the moderating effect of the World Bank’s Governance Indicators on the relationship between a firm’s ESG scores and its financial and market performance.
Methodology- To achieve the aim of the study, we have collected data for all listed firms from the European continent with ESG scores available on the Refinitiv database. After cleaning the data for missing values, we obtained an unbalanced and cross-sectional panel of 13,043 firm-year observations from the 2,083 firms used in the study. We have employed 2SLS Regression, using published financial information spanning over a period of 12 years, from 2011 to 2022.
Findings- The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance.
Conclusion- Our findings suggest that the positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators. The implementation of ESG practices is generally valued by investors affecting positively the market performance, however, this may not be as strong in countries with high Governance scores where expectations for sustainable business practices are already high.

Keywords: Europe, ESG, financial performance, market performance, World Bank Governance Indicators

Title: THE IMPACT OF ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) ON THE ECONOMIC GROWTH OF ASEAN-5 COUNTRIES
Snippet: In fact, to the best of our knowledge, previous studies on ESG practices for economic growth in the ASEAN-5 context have not been done yet. Many studies only focus on ESG practices for economic growth in the United Kingdom and other Europe countries Avetisyan and Hockerts (2017), Eccles and Viviers (2011), Luo (2022), Zhang et al. (2022), Bannier et al. (2019), De Lucia et al. (2020), and Sassen et al. (2016). In fact, according to Mahi et al. (2020), ASEAN-5 countries have the fastest-growing emerging markets compared to other countries. Therefore, studying ESG performance and economic growth among ASEAN-5 countries is pertinent. Besides that, ESG is a relatively new development concept that previous scholars and researchers have addressed as a broad term for sustainable development; this study contributes to the literature by constructing a new ESG country index and determining their effects on economic growth in ASEAN-5 countries. Billio et al. (2021) explored the disagreement between ESG rating agencies and its consequences on identifying ESG index constituents. This issue is pertinent given the absence of data and the limited availability of reliable information on the present ESG index. Thus, this study uses a text-mining approach to construct an ESG country index score and assess the impact of ESG on economic growth in the ASEAN-5 countries. This study will employ data mining techniques, specifically the text mining word frequency statistic, to analyze news articles related to ESG. This will help to gauge the level of attention given to ESG issues. 

This study provides three approaches. First, the study constructs an ESG country index score that better reflects the evolution of ESG throughout the ASEAN-5 countries. By using Google Trend analytics (which provides access to a large sample of search requests), it is possible to observe the evolution of ESG on economic growth in the ASEAN-5 countries. Second, the ARDL method was employed to establish the relationship between ESG and economic growth. Third, the study reviews the changes in the economic cycle or shock, particularly the pandemic crisis.

Economic performance, encompassing indicators like GDP growth, unemployment rates, and income distribution, significantly shapes a country's capacity to tackle environmental issues, foster social equity, and maintain effective governance standards. Yet, the existing gap between economic factors and ESG metrics hampers policymakers' and stakeholders' capacity to devise efficient strategies for sustainable development and inclusive growth. Each of these economic variables/indicators is considered crucial for understanding various aspects of economic health. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a comprehensive measure of a country's economic activity, reflecting overall growth and productivity. documents.title: Country governance scores as moderators of ESG impact on firm performance in the European context
documents.snippet:
Purpose- Engaging in ESG activities entails significant costs that, without a doubt, impact the firm's financial performance and ultimately its market performance. However, it is believed that these costs are offset by the positive impact ESG brings in terms of improved reputation and public perception, including current and potential customers and investors. Research on the relationship between ESG scores and firm performance has produced mixed results, raising concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs, or whether there are other factors that may moderate this relationship. The purpose of this study is to explore the moderating effect of the World Bank’s Governance Indicators on the relationship between a firm’s ESG scores and its financial and market performance.
Methodology- To achieve the aim of the study, we have collected data for all listed firms from the European continent with ESG scores available on the Refinitiv database. After cleaning the data for missing values, we obtained an unbalanced and cross-sectional panel of 13,043 firm-year observations from the 2,083 firms used in the study. We have employed 2SLS Regression, using published financial information spanning over a period of 12 years, from 2011 to 2022.
Findings- The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance.
Conclusion- Our findings suggest that the positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators. The implementation of ESG practices is generally valued by investors affecting positively the market performance, however, this may not be as strong in countries with high Governance scores where expectations for sustainable business practices are already high.

Title: Financial development measurement: Comparison of the high- and low-income countries
Snippet: For researchers aiming to reveal the impact of the financial sector on economic growth or any other economic phenomena, the first question to think about is which indicator should be used to estimate the development of the financial sector. The literature shows divergences in financial development proxies used which have prompted the International Monetary Fund (IMF) staff to create an indicator that includes all aspects of financial sector development. A financial development index (FD index) or an index of development of the financial sector is an index developed by the IMF staff which shows the level of development of financial institutions and financial markets in terms of depth, accessibility, and efficiency. This index includes all aspects of the development of the financial sector such as financial institutions and financial markets. 

There is extensive literature that explores the impact of the development of the financial sector on various economic phenomena focusing on a specific country or region. During the analysis of the literature, we notice the application of different methodologies, but what interests us, in this case, is the variability in terms of the variable which expresses the development of the financial sector or any aspect of it. Financial development, respectively banking sector development is measured by different proxies, but the most frequently used one is Private Credit as % of GDP (Rajan & Zingales, 1998 The primary aim of this paper is to present the problem of the lack of a financial development measurement single indicator and then using a single indicator, such as the FD index and its sub-components, a financial institutions index (FI index) and a financial markets index (FM index), to compare the financial development of high-and low-income countries. As to the main aim presented above the objectives of this research are to show the different indicators used to estimate the development of the financial sector, which are the most used in the literature, and the final and most important objective is to compare the financial development of high-and low-income countries by using the FD index and some other indicators.
